# Client Bio

![ADCCEEW Logo](aussiegov.png)

[The Australian Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water](https://www.dcceew.gov.au) develops national policies to reduce emissions and support Australia’s transition to a low-carbon economy. It leads efforts to address climate change while protecting the nation’s unique environment, biodiversity, water resources, and cultural heritage.

# Recommendation

The analysis shows economic growth can align with lower emissions and identifies coal as the primary driver of Australia’s carbon footprint. The ADCCEEW should support a shift to a low-emissions economy— for example, by introducing carbon pricing to drive cleaner practices, upgrading coal plant efficiency, and expanding clean energy industries to diversify supply.


# Evidence

## IDA

```{r ida, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, chunk_title = "IDA", results='hide'}

# IDA :D

library(ggplot2)
library(tidyverse)
library(dplyr)
library(maps)
library(plotly)

data <- read.csv("owid-co2-data.csv")

# Overview of the dataset
str(data)

# Display first few rows
head(data)

# Removing rows with missing values
data_clean <- na.omit(data)

# Removing "World" row
data_clean <- data_clean %>%
  filter(country != "World")

# Keep only most prosperous countries based on CO2 emissions per GDP
data_clean_filtered <- data_clean %>%
  filter(country %in% c("Switzerland", "Sweden", "United Kingdom", "Denmark", "France", "Australia"))

```

This dataset from [Our World in Data](https://ourworldindata.org/co2-and-other-greenhouse-gas-emissions) covers carbon dioxide (CO~2~) emissions and related economic metrics globally. A subset of countries (Switzerland, Sweden, UK, Denmark, France) was chosen for their low CO~2~ per GDP. This selection is supported by the dataset (as illustrated below) and external research ([GreenMatch, 2024](https://www.greenmatch.co.uk/blog/greenest-countries)). Despite differences in size and resources, these nations will provide valuable insights.

```{r map, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, results = 'axis'}

# --- Figuring out which countries to focus on ---
# Load map data
world_map <- map_data("world")

# Prepare CO2 per GDP data for the year 2022
co2_map_data <- data_clean %>%
  filter(year == 2022) %>%
  select(country, co2_per_gdp) %>%
  mutate(country = case_when(
    country == "United States" ~ "USA",
    country == "United Kingdom" ~ "UK",
    country == "Czechia" ~ "Czech Republic",
    TRUE ~ country  # else: keep original name
  ))

# Join map and CO₂ daat
map_df <- world_map %>%
  left_join(co2_map_data, by = c("region" = "country"))

# Plot
p <- ggplot(map_df, aes(long, lat, group = group, fill = co2_per_gdp, text = paste(region, ": ", round(co2_per_gdp, 3)))) +
  geom_polygon(color = "white") +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low = "darkgreen", high = "red", na.value = "grey90",
    name = "CO<sub>2</sub> per GDP"
  ) +
  labs(title = "CO<sub>2</sub> Emissions per GDP (2022)") +
  theme_minimal()

# Convert to interactive Plotly plot
ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text")

```

## Report


```{r gdpvco2, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE}

library(ggrepel)
library(scales)

# Filter GDP and CO2 data for years 2000 and 2022
gdp_co2_data <- data_clean_filtered %>%
  filter(year %in% c(2000, 2022)) %>%
  select(country, year, gdp, co2)

slope_data <- gdp_co2_data %>%
  # Each row is one country
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = c(gdp, co2)) %>%
  mutate(co2_diff = co2_2022 - co2_2000) %>%
  # One row per country-year pair
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("gdp_"), names_to = "year", values_to = "gdp") %>%
  mutate(year = gsub("gdp_", "", year),
         year = as.integer(year)) %>%
  select(country, year, gdp, co2_diff)

# Plot
ggplot(slope_data, aes(x = factor(year), y = gdp / 1e9, group = country)) +
  geom_line(aes(color = co2_diff), linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(aes(color = co2_diff), size = 3) +
  geom_text_repel(data = slope_data %>% filter(year == 2022), aes(label = country), nudge_x = 0.4) +
  scale_color_gradient2(
    low = "darkgreen", mid = "grey80", high = "red", midpoint = 0,
    name = expression("CO"[2]*" Change (2000–2022)")
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_number(suffix = "B"), limits = c(0, 3000)) +
  labs(
    title = expression("GDP Change Between 2000 & 2022 with CO"[2]*" Trends"),
    x = "Year", y = "GDP (Int$)",
    caption = expression("Green = CO"[2]*" reduction, Red = CO"[2]*" increase")
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```

Outliers like economic downturns are assumed to impact all the countries to a similar extent.

The UK and France clearly demonstrate that **economic growth can be decoupled from carbon emissions**. Both saw their GDP rise and CO~2~ output fall. Denmark, Sweden, and Switzerland too achieved this (albeit to a smaller extent).

In contrast, Australia is the only country to increase CO2 emissions while nearly doubling GDP, reflecting continued reliance on carbon-intensive energy ([CSIRO, 2024](https://www.csiro.au/en/research/environmental-impacts/climate-change/climate-change-qa/sources-of-co2)).


```{r pie, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(gganimate)

# Prepare long-format data
emissions_long <- data_clean_filtered %>%
  select(country, year, co2, flaring_co2, gas_co2, cement_co2, coal_co2, oil_co2, other_industry_co2) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -c(country, year, co2), names_to = "emission_type", values_to = "co2_value") %>%
  group_by(country, year) %>%
  mutate(proportion = co2_value / co2) %>%
  ungroup()

# Create pie charts (1 per country per year)
p <- ggplot(emissions_long, aes(x = "", y = proportion, fill = emission_type)) +
  geom_bar(width = 1, stat = "identity", color = "white") +
  coord_polar(theta = "y") +
  facet_wrap(~country) +
  labs(
    title = "CO2 Emission Type Proportions by Country",
    subtitle = "Year: {frame_time}",
    fill = "Emission Type"
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  transition_time(year)

# Animate
animate(p, renderer = gifski_renderer())

```

The above emissions categories are assumed to capture all major sources.

Coal remains central to Australia’s economy, dominating emissions. It is the largest source of electricity generation and the second-largest export earner. ([Whitehaven Coal, 2019](https://whitehavencoal.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/coal-hard-facts-minerals-council-australia.pdf))

In contrast, other developed countries have diversified their energy systems, with oil as the primary emissions source. **Coal is more carbon-intensive than oil or gas** ([ClientEarth, 2025](https://www.clientearth.org/latest/news/fossil-fuels-and-climate-change-the-facts/)). 

Switzerland stands out with near-zero coal use due to hydro-powered electricity  ([Climate Action Tracker, 2024](https://climateactiontracker.org/countries/switzerland/policies-action/)). The UK too has phased out coal in power generation ([Ember, 2025](https://ember-energy.org/app/uploads/2025/02/Clean-Power-2030-builds-stability-by-cutting-import-reliance.pdf)). 


::: panel-tabset

### CO~2~ Emissions per unit Energy

```{r}
# Line plot
p <- ggplot(data_clean_filtered, aes(x = year, y = co2_per_unit_energy, color = country)) +
   geom_line() +
   theme_minimal() +
   labs(title = "CO<sub>2</sub> Emissions per unit Energy Over Time by Country",
     x = "Year", 
     y = "CO<sub>2</sub> Emissions per Unit Energy")

ggplotly(p)

```

Australia’s CO~2~ emissions per unit of energy remains above peers (dropping just 13.8%). This reflects a slower shift to cleaner energy sources.

Denmark, once similar, cut intensity by 45.6% through wind and coal phase-out ([IEA, 2023](https://www.iea.org/reports/denmark-2023/executive-summary)). Sweden consistently had the lowest emissions intensity, with 70% renewable energy in 2024 ([Nowtricity, 2024](https://www.nowtricity.com/country/sweden/)).


### CO~2~ Emissions per Capita

```{r}
# Line plot
p <- ggplot(data_clean_filtered, aes(x = year, y = co2_per_capita, color = country)) +
   geom_line() +
   theme_minimal() +
   labs(title = "CO<sub>2</sub> Emissions per Capita Over Time by Country", 
     x = "Year", 
     y = "CO<sub>2</sub> Emissions per Capital")

ggplotly(p)

```

Australia also has the **highest per capita emissions**, peaking at ~19 tons (2004–2008), down to 14.6 tons by 2022. This shows a **high individual carbon footprint**.

All countries show a **downward trend** since 2007, signaling global progress and growing environmental awareness.

:::

## Limitations

-   Recent emission drops may reflect temporary COVID-19 effects, not structural change.
-   Imported emissions are excluded from this analysis, potentially understating true footprints.
-   GDP-adjusted values rely on potentially inaccurate PPP estimates.


# Ethics Statement

This project upholds the Shared Value of **truthfulness** by accurately presenting findings about the emissions & GDP data and acknowledging its limitations. It also adheres to the Ethical Principle of **avoiding preempted outcomes** by allowing the data to guide conclusions, rather than shaping findings to meet expectations or desired narratives.
